title: Granada Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Granada wells have a 64 ft median depth, but records range to 950 ft. See yield, water levels, drilling costs and local risks.
h1: Granada, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Granada means looking beyond the presence of a well permit. Local records show a median well depth of 64 feet, but the full range is wide, reaching 950 feet. Most recorded wells are shallow, and the area’s plains geology produces very different results from lot to lot.

Yield records are unusually strong, with a median reported pump yield of 113 gallons per minute. That figure comes from only 22 wells, so it should not be treated as a guarantee for a new domestic well. Use the nearby records as a screening tool, then verify the specific parcel, aquifer, well construction, and water rights before closing.

sections.heading: Granada well depths depend on the local formation
sections.html:
Within five miles of Granada, 77% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. The middle half runs from 46 to 89 feet, which gives a driller a reasonable starting range for a shallow plains-sediment bid. That range is not a promise. The records also include wells from 300 to 600 feet, wells deeper than 600 feet, and a deepest record of 950 feet.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. A smaller number identify the Cheyenne Sandstone or Dakota aquifers, and no recorded wells identify a Denver Basin aquifer. Ask for a written bid that explains what happens if the hole must continue past the expected formation or needs additional casing and grout.

sections.heading: Recorded yields are high, but the sample is small
sections.html:
The reported yield median near Granada is 113 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 22.5 to 1,225 gallons per minute. Of the wells that report a yield, 86% produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 5% fall in the one-to-five gallon range and none are recorded under one gallon per minute.

Those results are encouraging for irrigation and stock uses, but only 22 wells report a pump yield. A domestic buyer should not size a house system from the local median alone. Confirm the permit’s allowed use, test the well, and ask whether the pumping rate is a short test result or a dependable operating rate. Exempt household-use wells still have Colorado pumping limits and use restrictions.

sections.heading: Water levels vary widely in Granada records
sections.html:
Only 11 wells in the records report a static water level. Their median depth to water is 190 feet, with the middle half ranging from 23 to 287 feet. That spread shows why a nearby well’s water level may not predict the level at a particular lot, especially where well depths and named formations differ.

The permit counts by decade do not establish a groundwater trend. They show activity from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025, but they are not a time series of static water measurements. For a purchase, obtain the well construction report, static level, pumping information, and any available nearby measurements rather than assuming the water table is rising or dropping.

sections.heading: Permit history points to long local drilling experience
sections.html:
Granada’s permit record contains 258 wells, with 172 recorded as constructed and 174 reporting a total depth. The permits cover household, stock, irrigation, and monitoring uses. Irrigation accounts for 60% of the listed use mix, followed by stock at 15% and domestic or household use at 12%.

The most active names in these records are Ark Valley Pump & Supply, associated with Smith Jr., William, with 20 wells; Hoffman, associated with Hoffman, Earl, with 11; and Authorized, associated with Pe, Pg, with 9. These records can help identify local experience, but they do not rank current workmanship. Check licensing, references, the proposed construction method, and who will service the pump after completion.

sections.heading: A shallow Granada well may still cost more than expected
sections.html:
For Granada’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 64 feet, the drilled hole models to about $2,200 to $3,500. That is only the hole. A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,200 to $15,500.

Get the driller to separate drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, electrical work, trenching, testing, and permit-related work. A deep outlier, difficult access, extra casing, or a change in formation can move the price above the shallow-hole estimate. The middle-half depth range of 46 to 89 feet is useful for comparison shopping, not a fixed bid.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic layout, and dry-hole exposure
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove a parcel’s water is unsafe, but it is enough reason to test before relying on the well. Review the well location, casing and grout, nearby land uses, and any available laboratory results.

Low yield is not the only concern. A dry hole, poor construction, pump failure, or unsuitable water quality can affect a building budget. Confirm that the proposed septic field, replacement area, driveway, and house site can fit with the well and required separation distances. In an over-appropriated basin, ask the Colorado Division of Water Resources about augmentation and the permitted use before planning additional domestic, irrigation, or livestock demands.

sections.heading: What to verify before buying near Granada
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s permit number and construction report, then compare nearby wells in Granada, Hartman, Holly, Lamar, Wiley, Brandon, and Sheridan Lake where records are relevant. Pay closest attention to wells with the same intended use and similar depth or aquifer. A high reported yield in an irrigation record does not automatically establish a reliable household supply.

Before closing, confirm the permit status, legal use, well location, production test, static water level, water-quality test, and pump condition. If the lot has no well, obtain a site-specific drilling estimate and ask what happens if the first target is unproductive. For a new build, coordinate well, septic, electrical, access, and house placement before excavation. That sequence can prevent a workable lot from becoming an expensive redesign.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Granada, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth near Granada is 64 feet, and the middle half runs from 46 to 89 feet. Still, the records include much deeper wells: 11% are from 300 to 600 feet, 10% are deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 950 feet. Local geology and the target aquifer matter more than the median alone.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Granada?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 64-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,200 to $3,500. A completed system, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at $8,200 to $15,500. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing, and site conditions can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Granada wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 22 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 113 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 22.5 to 1,225 gallons per minute, and 86% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Most of these records are not household wells, so a buyer should verify the specific well’s test, permitted use, and dependable operating rate.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Granada, Colorado?
faq.a: The records identify 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped sites do not determine a particular well’s quality. Test the water before purchase, review the well construction, and consider site history, especially near known environmental areas.

faq.q: Are Granada wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available data does not establish a declining water table. Only 11 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 190 feet and a middle half from 23 to 287 feet. Permit counts by decade are not water-level measurements. For a property decision, obtain the specific well’s static level, pumping information, and recent test results.
